name: Health and Life Sciences
blurb: Clinicians, health system executives and drug discovery leaders applying AI to medicine.

reading.body:
AI in healthcare moves upstream and downstream simultaneously: drug discovery leaders like Zhavoronkov use generative models to design novel molecules from scratch, while hospital innovators like Schwartz must solve the harder problem of making clinicians trust and use AI tools at the bedside.

The field splits along a fundamental divide. On one side, computational researchers apply foundation models and agentic frameworks directly to biology, treating drug discovery as a machine learning problem where AI can generate candidates faster than human chemists. On the other side, health system leaders face the unglamorous work of data interoperability, clinician adoption, and governance, the invisible infrastructure that determines whether an AI tool lives or dies in practice.

This split matters because neither side scales without the other. A drug designed by AI still needs clinical validation, regulatory pathways, and hospital systems equipped to deploy it. A hospital with perfect AI tools cannot prove their value without a pipeline of validated treatments to support. The constraint is not algorithmic but organizational: the people who understand both medicine and systems change remain scarce, which is why experienced figures from policy, operations, and computational biology are moving into these roles. This data covers leadership profiles and does not measure adoption rates, failure costs, or the actual time from AI discovery to patient care, so it cannot quantify how severe the bottleneck remains.

profiles.hook: Zhavoronkov built Insilico Medicine to prove that generative AI could do more than analyze biology, it could design new drug candidates outright, and Rentosertib, discovered and designed by Insilico's AI pipeline, became one of the first such molecules to reach human clinical trials.
